question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y)=x y + 2 x$, where $x=\left(t - 1\right) e^{t - 1}$ and $y=s e^{t - 1}$. Calculate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
![Chain-rule paths to s](images/21/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

Hold $t$ fixed. Multiply along each path to $s$, then add the two products.

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial s}
$$

First find the outer partial derivatives, treating $x$ and $y$ as independent.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=y + 2, \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Write the outer partial derivatives in terms of $s$ and $t$.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=s e^{t - 1} + 2, \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=\left(t - 1\right) e^{t - 1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next differentiate the intermediate variables with respect to $s$, holding $t$ fixed.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s}&=0, \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial s}&=e^{t - 1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute into the chain rule and simplify the products and sum.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}&=\left(s e^{t - 1} + 2\right)\left(0\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(\left(t - 1\right) e^{t - 1}\right)\left(e^{t - 1}\right) \\ &=\left(t - 1\right) e^{2 t - 2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y)=x y$, where $x=\cos{\left(s \left(t - 1\right) \right)}$ and $y=\sin{\left(s \left(t - 1\right) \right)}$. Calculate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}$.

Hold $s$ fixed. Multiply along each path to $t$, then add the two products.

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}
$$

First find the outer partial derivatives, treating $x$ and $y$ as independent.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=y, \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Write the outer partial derivatives in terms of $s$ and $t$.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=\sin{\left(s \left(t - 1\right) \right)}, \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=\cos{\left(s \left(t - 1\right) \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next differentiate the intermediate variables with respect to $t$, holding $s$ fixed.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial x}{\partial t}&=- s \sin{\left(s \left(t - 1\right) \right)}, \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial t}&=s \cos{\left(s \left(t - 1\right) \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute into the chain rule and simplify the products and sum.

\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}&=\left(\sin{\left(s \left(t - 1\right) \right)}\right)\left(- s \sin{\left(s \left(t - 1\right) \right)}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(\cos{\left(s \left(t - 1\right) \right)}\right)\left(s \cos{\left(s \left(t - 1\right) \right)}\right) \\ &=s \left(- \sin^{2}{\left(s \left(t - 1\right) \right)} + \cos^{2}{\left(s \left(t - 1\right) \right)}\right).\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y)=\ln{\left(x^{2} + y^{2} \right)}$, where $x=\left(t + 1\right) e^{- s}$ and $y=\left(t + 1\right) e^{s}$. Calculate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}$. Work where $t + 1\ne 0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
![Chain-rule paths to t](images/11/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

Hold $s$ fixed. Multiply along each path to $t$, then add the two products.

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}
$$

First find the outer partial derivatives, treating $x$ and $y$ as independent.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=\frac{2 x}{x^{2} + y^{2}}, \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=\frac{2 y}{x^{2} + y^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Factor the common denominator before substituting into the outer partial derivatives.

$$
\begin{aligned}x^2+y^2&=\left(t + 1\right)^{2} \left(e^{2 s} + e^{- 2 s}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Cancel the common nonzero coordinate factor when writing the outer partial derivatives in terms of $s$ and $t$.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=\frac{2 e^{- s}}{\left(t + 1\right) \left(e^{2 s} + e^{- 2 s}\right)}, \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=\frac{2 e^{s}}{\left(t + 1\right) \left(e^{2 s} + e^{- 2 s}\right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next differentiate the intermediate variables with respect to $t$, holding $s$ fixed.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial x}{\partial t}&=e^{- s}, \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial t}&=e^{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute into the chain rule and simplify the products and sum.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}&=\left(\frac{2 e^{- s}}{\left(t + 1\right) \left(e^{2 s} + e^{- 2 s}\right)}\right)\left(e^{- s}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(\frac{2 e^{s}}{\left(t + 1\right) \left(e^{2 s} + e^{- 2 s}\right)}\right)\left(e^{s}\right) \\ &=\frac{2}{t + 1}.\end{aligned}
$$

:answer-field/choices.:answer/value: \frac{2 \left(2 e^{2 s} + e^{- 2 s}\right)}{\left(t + 1\right) \left(e^{2 s} + e^{- 2 s}\right)}
\frac{2 \left(e^{2 s} + 2 e^{- 2 s}\right)}{\left(t + 1\right) \left(e^{2 s} + e^{- 2 s}\right)}

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y)=x y$, where $x=\sin{\left(s \right)}$ and $y=\sin{\left(t - 1 \right)} + \cos{\left(s \right)}$. Calculate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}$.

Hold $t$ fixed. Multiply along each path to $s$, then add the two products.

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial s}
$$

First find the outer partial derivatives, treating $x$ and $y$ as independent.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=y, \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Write the outer partial derivatives in terms of $s$ and $t$.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=\sin{\left(t - 1 \right)} + \cos{\left(s \right)}, \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=\sin{\left(s \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next differentiate the intermediate variables with respect to $s$, holding $t$ fixed.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s}&=\cos{\left(s \right)}, \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial s}&=- \sin{\left(s \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute into the chain rule and simplify the products and sum.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}&=\left(\sin{\left(t - 1 \right)} + \cos{\left(s \right)}\right)\left(\cos{\left(s \right)}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(\sin{\left(s \right)}\right)\left(- \sin{\left(s \right)}\right) \\ &=\left(\sin{\left(t - 1 \right)} + \cos{\left(s \right)}\right) \cos{\left(s \right)} - \sin^{2}{\left(s \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y)=x y^{2}$, where $x=s - t + 1$ and $y=s \left(t - 1\right)$. Calculate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}$.

$$

First find the outer partial derivatives, treating $x$ and $y$ as independent.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=y^{2}, \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=2 x y.\end{aligned}
$$

Write the outer partial derivatives in terms of $s$ and $t$.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=s^{2} \left(t - 1\right)^{2}, \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=2 s \left(t - 1\right) \left(s - t + 1\right).\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}&=\left(s^{2} \left(t - 1\right)^{2}\right)\left(-1\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(2 s \left(t - 1\right) \left(s - t + 1\right)\right)\left(s\right) \\ &=s^{2} \left(t - 1\right) \left(2 s - 3 t + 3\right).\end{aligned}

Write these partials in terms of $s$ and $t$:

$$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
Let $f(x,y,z)=\frac{- 2 x - z}{y}$, where $x=t^{2}$, $y=s + t$, $z=s^{2}$. Assume $s+t \ne 0$. Given that

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}=\frac{c_{1} s^{2} + c_{2} s t + c_{3} t^{2}}{\left(s + t\right)^{2}}
$$

find the value of $c_1+c_2+c_3$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/b5/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

Hold $s$ fixed. Multiply along the three paths and add:

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \frac{\partial x}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \frac{\partial y}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial t}
$$

First find the outer partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=- \frac{2}{y} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=- \frac{- 2 x - z}{y^{2}} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=- \frac{1}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Write these partials in terms of $s$ and $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=- \frac{2}{s + t} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=- \frac{- s^{2} - 2 t^{2}}{\left(s + t\right)^{2}} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=- \frac{1}{s + t}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiate each intermediate variable with respect to $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial x}{\partial t}&=2 t \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial t}&=1 \\ \frac{\partial z}{\partial t}&=0\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the matching factors, then collect terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}&=\left(- \frac{2}{s + t}\right)\left(2 t\right) \\ &{}+\left(- \frac{- s^{2} - 2 t^{2}}{\left(s + t\right)^{2}}\right)\left(1\right) \\ &{}+\left(- \frac{1}{s + t}\right)\left(0\right) \\ &=\frac{s^{2} - 4 s t - 2 t^{2}}{\left(s + t\right)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Match the coefficients with the supplied expression:

$$
c_{1}=1,\quad c_{2}=-4,\quad c_{3}=-2
$$

Therefore

$$
c_1+c_2+c_3=1+\left(-4\right)+\left(-2\right)=-5.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let $f(x,y,z)=x y + 3 x z + 2 z^{2}$, where $x=\frac{t}{s}$, $y=s^{2} + t^{2}$, $z=s^{2} t$. Assume $s \ne 0$. Given that

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}=c_{1} s + c_{2} s t + c_{3} s^{4} t + \frac{3 t^{2}}{s}
$$

find the value of $c_1+c_2+c_3$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/b5/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

Hold $s$ fixed. Multiply along the three paths and add:

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \frac{\partial x}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \frac{\partial y}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial t}
$$

First find the outer partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=y + 3 z \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=x \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=3 x + 4 z\end{aligned}
$$

Write these partials in terms of $s$ and $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=3 s^{2} t + s^{2} + t^{2} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=\frac{t}{s} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=4 s^{2} t + \frac{3 t}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiate each intermediate variable with respect to $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial x}{\partial t}&=\frac{1}{s} \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial t}&=2 t \\ \frac{\partial z}{\partial t}&=s^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the matching factors, then collect terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}&=\left(3 s^{2} t + s^{2} + t^{2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{s}\right) \\ &{}+\left(\frac{t}{s}\right)\left(2 t\right) \\ &{}+\left(4 s^{2} t + \frac{3 t}{s}\right)\left(s^{2}\right) \\ &=\frac{4 s^{5} t + 6 s^{2} t + s^{2} + 3 t^{2}}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Match the coefficients with the supplied expression:

$$
c_{1}=1,\quad c_{2}=6,\quad c_{3}=4
$$

Therefore

$$
c_1+c_2+c_3=1+6+4=11.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let $f(x,y,z)=x y^{2} + \cos{\left(z \right)}$, where $x=- 2 s t$, $y=- 2 s - 2 t$, $z=3 s$. Given that

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}=c_{1} s^{2} t + c_{2} s t^{2} + c_{3} t^{3} - 3 \sin{\left(3 s \right)}
$$

find the value of $c_1+c_2+c_3$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/be/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

Hold $t$ fixed. Multiply along the three paths and add:

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \frac{\partial x}{\partial s}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \frac{\partial y}{\partial s}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial s}
$$

First find the outer partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=y^{2} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=2 x y \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=- \sin{\left(z \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Write these partials in terms of $s$ and $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=\left(- 2 s - 2 t\right)^{2} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=- 4 s t \left(- 2 s - 2 t\right) \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=- \sin{\left(3 s \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiate each intermediate variable with respect to $s$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s}&=- 2 t \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial s}&=-2 \\ \frac{\partial z}{\partial s}&=3\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the matching factors, then collect terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}&=\left(\left(- 2 s - 2 t\right)^{2}\right)\left(- 2 t\right) \\ &{}+\left(- 4 s t \left(- 2 s - 2 t\right)\right)\left(-2\right) \\ &{}+\left(- \sin{\left(3 s \right)}\right)\left(3\right) \\ &=- 24 s^{2} t - 32 s t^{2} - 8 t^{3} - 3 \sin{\left(3 s \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Match the coefficients with the supplied expression:

$$
c_{1}=-24,\quad c_{2}=-32,\quad c_{3}=-8
$$

Therefore

$$
c_1+c_2+c_3=\left(-24\right)+\left(-32\right)+\left(-8\right)=-64.
$$

question.:question/problem: For which of the following vector fields is $f(x,y)=- x^{2} - 4 y$ a potential function?
question.:question/worked-solution:
A vector field $F$ is conservative if it is the gradient of a scalar function $f.$ That is, there exists a function $f$ such that $F=\nabla f.$ The function $f$ is called a potential function for $F.$

To compute the vector field associated with a potential function $f,$ we compute its gradient:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f &=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,i+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\,j \\ &=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(- x^{2} - 4 y\right)\,i+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(- x^{2} - 4 y\right)\,j \\ &=-2 x\,i-4\,j \\ &=F\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector field that has $f$ as a potential function is

$$
F=-2 x\,i-4\,j.
$$

question.:question/problem: For which of the following vector fields is $f(x,y,z)=- x y e^{2 x z} + 2 z^{2}$ a potential function?
question.:question/worked-solution:
A potential function satisfies $F=\nabla f$. Differentiate with respect to each coordinate, holding the others constant.

For $f_x$, both factors of $- x y e^{2 x z}$ depend on $x$, so the product and chain rules give

$$
f_x=- ye^{2 x z}+(- x y)(2 z)e^{2 x z}.
$$

For $f_y$, the exponential is constant. For $f_z$, apply the chain rule to the exponential and differentiate the added quadratic. Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x&=- 2 x y z e^{2 x z} - y e^{2 x z} \\ f_y&=- x e^{2 x z} \\ f_z&=- 2 x^{2} y e^{2 x z} + 4 z\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the components in $x,y,z$ order,

$$
F=\begin{aligned}&-\left(1 y e^{2 x z}+2 x y z e^{2 x z}\right)\,i-1 x e^{2 x z}\,j \\ &-\left(-4 z+2 x^{2} y e^{2 x z}\right)\,k\end{aligned}.
$$

\begin{aligned}&-\left(1 y e^{2 x z}+2 x y z e^{2 x z}\right)\,i-1 x e^{2 x z}\,j \\ &-\left(-4 z+2 x^{2} y e^{2 x z}\right)\,k\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following vector fields are conservative on $\mathbb R^2$? Select all that apply.

For $\mathbf V=P\,\mathbf i+Q\,\mathbf j$ with continuous first partial derivatives on $\mathbb R^2$, the field is conservative exactly when $P_y=Q_x$ everywhere. The partial derivatives are supplied:

| Field | $P_y$ | $Q_x$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\mathbf F$ | $-2$ | $-2$ |
| $\mathbf G$ | $- 6 x y^{2}$ | $- 6 x y^{2}$ |
| $\mathbf H$ | $2 x$ | $4 x$ |
question.:question/worked-solution:
All components have continuous first partial derivatives on $\mathbb R^2$. Polynomial, exponential, trigonometric and arctangent functions are smooth here; any logarithm has positive argument and any denominator is strictly positive. Thus $\mathbf V=P\,\mathbf i+Q\,\mathbf j$ is **conservative** exactly when $P_y=Q_x$ everywhere.

For $\mathbf F$, differentiate each component with respect to the indicated variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}P&=- 2 x - 2 y,\\Q&=- 2 x - 2 y - 1,\\P_y&=-2,\\Q_x&=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

$P_y=Q_x$ is an identity, so $\mathbf F$ is conservative.

For $\mathbf G$, differentiate each component with respect to the indicated variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}P&=- 2 x y^{3} + x - 1,\\Q&=- 3 x^{2} y^{2} + y - 1,\\P_y&=- 6 x y^{2},\\Q_x&=- 6 x y^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$P_y=Q_x$ is an identity, so $\mathbf G$ is conservative.

For $\mathbf H$, differentiate each component with respect to the indicated variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}P&=2 x y - 2 x,\\Q&=2 x^{2} - 2 y + 1,\\P_y&=2 x,\\Q_x&=4 x.\end{aligned}
$$

The derivatives are not equal everywhere, so $\mathbf H$ is not conservative. At $(1,0)$, the difference is $-2\ne0$.

Select $\mathbf F$, $\mathbf G$.

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: $\mathbf F=$ $\left(- 2 x - 2 y\right)\,\mathbf i$ $+\left(- 2 x - 2 y - 1\right)\,\mathbf j$
$\mathbf G=$ $\left(- 2 x y^{3} + x - 1\right)\,\mathbf i$ $+\left(- 3 x^{2} y^{2} + y - 1\right)\,\mathbf j$
$\mathbf H=$ $\left(2 x y - 2 x\right)\,\mathbf i$ $+\left(2 x^{2} - 2 y + 1\right)\,\mathbf j$

The matching terms cancel as identities. Any common factor that vanishes at some points is nonzero elsewhere; equality at those zeros alone would not determine the constant.

At $a=1$, the two displayed partial derivatives agree everywhere, so this value satisfies the conservative-field condition.

Write $\mathbf F=P\,\mathbf i+Q\,\mathbf j$. Both components have continuous first partial derivatives on $\mathbb R^2$. On this domain, the conservative-field test is $P_y=Q_x$ everywhere.

The required partial derivatives are
$$
\begin{aligned}P_y&=32 y x + 49 \\ Q_x&=2 a^{2} y x + \left(a + 3\right)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Equality is an identity in $x$ and $y$, so the coefficient of $xy$ and the constant term must both agree:
$$
\begin{aligned}a^2&=16 \\ \left(a + 3\right)^{2}&=49\end{aligned}
$$
The first condition gives $a=-4$ or $a=4$. The second gives $a=4$ or $a=-10$. Their only common value is $a=4$. The opposite root of the first condition fails the constant-term condition; the other root of the second fails the coefficient condition.

At $a=4$, the two displayed partial derivatives agree everywhere, so this value satisfies the conservative-field condition.

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Domain of a Vector Field

question.:question/problem:
Determine the domain of the real vector field

$$
F(x,y)=x^{2}\,i+\left(\frac{1}{y + 1}\right)\,j.
$$

Remember: both component functions must be defined.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $F=P\,i+Q\,j$, where

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y)&=x^{2}\\Q(x,y)&=\frac{1}{y + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

P: This polynomial is defined everywhere in the real plane.

Thus $D_P=\mathbb R^2$.

Q: Every denominator must be nonzero, including a square root in a denominator.

The required conditions are $y + 1 \neq 0$.

Thus $D_Q=\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\,|\,y + 1 \neq 0\right\}$.

The domain is the intersection:

$$
\begin{aligned}D&=D_P\cap D_Q\\&=\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\,|\,y + 1 \neq 0\right\}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
A vector field on $\mathbb R^3$ assigns a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ to each point of a subset of $\mathbb R^3$.

Which of the following are vector fields on $\mathbb R^3$? Use each function's natural real domain. Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
A vector field on $\mathbb R^3$ assigns a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ to each point of a subset of $\mathbb R^3$.

Check each function's declared inputs and output vectors.

- **L.** $L(t)$ takes one real parameter. Its output has $2$ coordinates and is a vector in $\mathbb R^2$. All components are defined on $\mathbb R$. It **is not** a vector field on $\mathbb R^3$ because its declared inputs are not points of $\mathbb R^3$ and its outputs are not vectors in $\mathbb R^3$.

- **V.** $V(x,y)$ takes points in $\mathbb R^2$. Its output has $3$ coordinates and is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$. A denominator must be nonzero. Its natural domain is
$$
S_{V}=\{(x,y)\in \mathbb R^2\mid x-2\ne0,\quad y-2\ne0\}.
$$
It **is not** a vector field on $\mathbb R^3$ because its declared inputs are not points of $\mathbb R^3$.

- **X.** $X(x,y,z)$ takes points in $\mathbb R^3$. Its three standard-basis coefficients give 
$$
X(x,y,z)=\langle x, y^2, z+x\rangle.
$$
All components are defined on $\mathbb R^3$. It maps its nonempty domain in $\mathbb R^3$ to vectors in $\mathbb R^3$, so it **is** a vector field on $\mathbb R^3$.

Select $X$.

knowledge_point.title: Calculating Flux Across Other Type I and Type II Regions

question.:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the **outward flux** of

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=\left\langle 2 x - \cos{\left(y \right)},\;- 2 y + e^{x}\right\rangle
$$

through the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(-1,1)$, and $(2,1)$.

Use the supplied bounds and formula:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\leq y\leq 1,\quad - y\leq x\leq 2 y\}
$$

![Shaded region and a representative integration slice.](region-f14b138215e33c1ca6.png)

$$
\Phi=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,dA.
$$

Select the flux.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The components have continuous first derivatives on a neighborhood of $D$. With $C=\partial D$ counterclockwise and $\mathbf n$ outward, Green\'s theorem gives

$$
\Phi=\oint_C P\,dy-Q\,dx=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,dA.
$$

Here $P=2 x - \cos{\left(y \right)}$ and $Q=- 2 y + e^{x}$, so

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}=2,\qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}=-2,\qquad \operatorname{div}\mathbf F=0.
$$

The lower vertex has $y=0$ and the top edge has $y=1$. Horizontal slices run between the two sloping sides, from $x=- y$ to $x=2 y$.

![Shaded region and a representative integration slice.](region-f14b138215e33c1ca6.png)

This is a type II region:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\leq y\leq 1,\quad - y\leq x\leq 2 y\}
$$

$$

The polynomial components have continuous first partial derivatives on a neighborhood of the enclosed region. The counterclockwise boundary has positive orientation.

The matching component derivatives are

$$

$$

Add these derivatives to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}&=(4 x y)+(4 x y)\\ &=8 x y.\end{aligned}

The triangle specifies $D$; no bounds are needed to identify its integrand.

question.:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the outward flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=\left\langle 3 x + y^{2},\ x^{3} + 2 y\right\rangle
$$

through the boundary of the rectangle $0\le x\le 1$, $1\le y\le 2$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $D$ be the rectangle, with $C=\partial D$ traversed counterclockwise and outward unit normal $\mathbf n$. Both components have continuous first derivatives near $D$. Green's theorem gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm{d}s\\
&=\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}y-Q\,\mathrm{d}x\\
&=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.
\end{aligned}
$$

The rectangular bounds are

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\ 1\le y\le 2\}.
$$

![Rectangle with x bounds 0, 1 and y bounds 1, 2](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/edb-math/repairs/2026-10-28-topic-audit-3/group-1/generated-assets/17592186172101/easy/rectangle-173872518c72d80c67fd.png)

Hold the other coordinate constant in each partial derivative. The cross-variable terms contribute zero.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}&=3,\\
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}&=2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the matching partials gives

$$
\operatorname{div}\mathbf F=5.
$$

Integrate with respect to $x$, subtract its endpoints, then integrate with respect to $y$ and subtract its endpoints.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\int_{1}^{2}\int_{0}^{1}\left(5\right)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=\int_{1}^{2}\left[5 x\right]_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=\int_{1}^{2}\left(5\right)\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=\left[5 y\right]_{y=1}^{y=2}\\
&=\left(10\right)-\left(5\right)\\
&=5.
\end{aligned}
$$

\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}&=- 6 x y,\\
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}&=- 3 x.
\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the matching partials gives

$$
\operatorname{div}\mathbf F=- 6 x y - 3 x.
$$

Integrate with respect to $x$, subtract its endpoints, then integrate with respect to $y$ and subtract its endpoints.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\int_{-2}^{-1}\int_{0}^{2}\left(- 6 x y - 3 x\right)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=\int_{-2}^{-1}\left[- 3 x^{2} y - \frac{3 x^{2}}{2}\right]_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=\int_{-2}^{-1}\left(- 12 y - 6\right)\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=\left[- 6 y^{2} - 6 y\right]_{y=-2}^{y=-1}\\
&=\left(0\right)-\left(-12\right)\\
&=12.
\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Calculating Flux Across Rectangles

question.:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the outward flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=\left\langle 2 x^{3} + y^{2},\ x^{3} - x y^{3}\right\rangle
$$

through the boundary of the rectangle with vertices $(-1,-1)$, $(2,-1)$, $(2,0)$, and $(-1,0)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $D$ be the rectangle, with $C=\partial D$ traversed counterclockwise and outward unit normal $\mathbf n$. Both components have continuous first derivatives near $D$. Green's theorem gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm{d}s\\
&=\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}y-Q\,\mathrm{d}x\\
&=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.
\end{aligned}
$$

The rectangular bounds are

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 2,\ -1\le y\le 0\}.
$$

![Rectangle with x bounds -1, 2 and y bounds -1, 0](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/edb-math/repairs/2026-10-28-topic-audit-3/group-1/generated-assets/17592186172101/hard/rectangle-74d43f8c8e808696465e.png)

Hold the other coordinate constant in each partial derivative. The cross-variable terms contribute zero.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}&=6 x^{2},\\
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}&=- 3 x y^{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the matching partials gives

$$
\operatorname{div}\mathbf F=6 x^{2} - 3 x y^{2}.
$$

Integrate with respect to $x$, subtract its endpoints, then integrate with respect to $y$ and subtract its endpoints.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\int_{-1}^{0}\int_{-1}^{2}\left(6 x^{2} - 3 x y^{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=\int_{-1}^{0}\left[2 x^{3} - \frac{3 x^{2} y^{2}}{2}\right]_{x=-1}^{x=2}\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=\int_{-1}^{0}\left(18 - \frac{9 y^{2}}{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=\left[- \frac{3 y^{3}}{2} + 18 y\right]_{y=-1}^{y=0}\\
&=\left(0\right)-\left(- \frac{33}{2}\right)\\
&=\frac{33}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem

question.:question/problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186175987/plots/ba6adc294b17d4e94ee5.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral

$$
\oint_C(2 y + \sin{\left(x \right)})\,dx+(3 x + \cos{\left(y \right)})\,dy\,?
$$

The cross partials are $\partial P/\partial y=2$ and $\partial Q/\partial x=3$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint_C P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,dA.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186175987/plots/248e7b39f1e866a52aac.png)

Since $P(x,y)=2 y + \sin{\left(x \right)}$ and $Q(x,y)=3 x + \cos{\left(y \right)},$ we obtain

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=2,\qquad\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=3.
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\oint_C(2 y + \sin{\left(x \right)})\,dx+(3 x + \cos{\left(y \right)})\,dy&=\iint_D(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y})\,dA\\&=\iint_D\left(3-\left(2\right)\right)\,dA\\&=\iint_D\left(1\right)\,dA.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le 6,\ 0\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint_D f(x,y)\,dA=\iint_\Delta f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta.
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D\left(1\right)\,dA&=\iint_\Delta\left(1\right)r\,dr\,d\theta\\&=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\int_{0}^{6}r\,dr\,d\theta.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186175987/plots/cdd95dd970a635a4e3a0.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y)=⟨5\left(y(x+1)\right),\,5\left(x(y+1)\right)⟩,$ which of the following is equivalent to ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr\,?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr=5\left({∮}_{C}y(x+1)\,dx+x(y+1)\,dy.\right)
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186175987/plots/6217be11548216cbab8d.png)

Since $P(x,y)=5\left(y(x+1)\right)$ and $Q(x,y)=5\left(x(y+1)\right),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=5\left(x+1\right),\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=5\left(y+1\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5\left({∮}_{C}y(x+1)\,dx+x(y+1)\,dy\right) & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =5\left({∬}_{D}(y+1-(x+1))\,\text{d}A\right) \\  & =5\left({∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A.\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 5,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that  

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}5\left({∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A\right) & =5\left({∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta \right) \\  & =5\left({\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{5}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta .\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\left({∮}_{C}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{y+1})\,dy\right) & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =4\left({∬}_{D}({y}^{2}-(-{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A\right) \\  & =4\left({∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}4\left({∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A\right) & =4\left({∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta \right) \\  & =4\left({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\,dr\,d\theta .\right)\end{aligned}

P(x,y)=\sqrt{x+1}-2x^2y,\quad Q(x,y)=e^y+2xy^2,
$$

we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=- 2 x^{2},\quad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=2 y^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\oint_C(\sqrt{x+1}-2x^2y)\,dx+(e^y+2xy^2)\,dy&=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,dA \\ &=\iint_D\left(2 y^{2}-(- 2 x^{2})\right)\,dA \\ &=\iint_D 2(x^2+y^2)\,dA.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le 5,0\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint_D f(x,y)\,dA=\iint_\Delta f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta.
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D 2(x^2+y^2)\,dA&=\iint_\Delta 2(r^2(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta))\,r\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\int_{0}^{5}r^3(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\int_{0}^{5}r^3\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left[\frac{r^4}{4}\right]_{0}^{5}\,d\theta \\ &=2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(\frac{625}{4}-0\right)\,d\theta \\ &=2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{625}{4}\,d\theta \\ &=\frac{625}{2}[\theta]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &=\frac{625}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-0\right) \\ &=\frac{625 \pi}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as $\oint_C F\cdot dr=\oint_C(2 x y^{2})\,dx+(5 x + e^{\cos{(y )}})\,dy$.

Applying Green's theorem, we get $\oint_C F\cdot dr=\iint_D(5-(4 x y))\,dA=\iint_D(- 4 x y + 5)\,dA$.

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as $\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le 4,0\le\theta\le2\pi\}$.

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that $\iint_D f(x,y)\,dA=\iint_\Delta f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)r\,dr\,d\theta$.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as $\iint_D(- 4 x y + 5)\,dA=\iint_\Delta(- 4 r^{2} \sin{(\theta )} \cos{(\theta )} + 5)r\,dr\,d\theta=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{4}r (- 2 r^{2} \sin{(2 \theta )} + 5)\,dr\,d\theta$.

\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(-15{x}^{2}-6{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(-15\cdot (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}-6\cdot (r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta \\ & ={∬}_{Δ}(-15{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -6{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta \\ & ={∬}_{Δ}(-15{r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -6{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{4}-15{r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -6{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

The curve $C$ is parameterized by $\mathbf r(t)=(t)\,\mathbf i+(2 t)\,\mathbf j$, $0\le t\le 2$. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F(x,y)=(4)\,\mathbf i+(-3)\,\mathbf j$ through $C$ with respect to the unit normal $\mathbf n$ shown. Gray field arrows indicate direction only.

*Hint:* Check the pictured normal against the tangent for increasing $t$. For a clockwise normal use $$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds=\int_a^b(Py\prime-Qx\prime)\,\mathrm dt.
$$
For an anticlockwise normal, negate this expression.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the supplied parameterization $x=t,\ y=2 t$, $0\le t\le 2$. It runs from $(0,0)$ to $(2,4)$.

The tangent has direction $(1,2)$. The pictured normal is its $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation, with direction $(2,-1)$.

![Tangent and selected normal](flux-e25f51a259ee995562f7-orientation.png)

Substitute the curve into the field and differentiate its coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x(t),y(t))&=4 \\
Q(x(t),y(t))&=-3 \\
x'&=1 \\
y'&=2\end{aligned}
$$

The clockwise normal permits the flux formula directly.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds&=\int_{0}^{2}(Py\prime-Qx\prime)\,\mathrm dt \\
&=\int_{0}^{2}\left[(4)(2)-(-3)(1)\right]\,\mathrm dt \\
&=\int_{0}^{2}(11)\,\mathrm dt \\
&=\left[11 t\right]_{0}^{2} \\
&=(22)-(0) \\
&=22\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the supplied parameterization $x=t^{2},\ y=t$, $0\le t\le 1$. It runs from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$.

The tangent has direction $(2 t,1)$. The pictured normal is its $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation, with direction $(1,- 2 t)$.

![Tangent and selected normal](flux-bd1a63e56f16a8a5107a-orientation.png)

Substitute the curve into the field and differentiate its coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x(t),y(t))&=3 \left(t\right)=3 t \\
Q(x(t),y(t))&=4 \left(t^{2}\right) - 1=4 t^{2} - 1 \\
x'&=2 t \\
y'&=1\end{aligned}
$$

The clockwise normal permits the flux formula directly.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds&=\int_{0}^{1}(Py\prime-Qx\prime)\,\mathrm dt \\
&=\int_{0}^{1}\left[(3 t)(1)-(4 t^{2} - 1)(2 t)\right]\,\mathrm dt \\
&=\int_{0}^{1}(- 8 t^{3} + 5 t)\,\mathrm dt \\
&=\left[- 2 t^{4} + \frac{5 t^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1} \\
&=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-(0) \\
&=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

The curve $C$ is parameterized by $\mathbf r(t)=(\ln{\left(t \right)})\,\mathbf i+(2 t)\,\mathbf j$, $1\le t\le e$. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F(x,y)=(- 3 e^{- x})\,\mathbf i+(2)\,\mathbf j$ through $C$ with respect to the unit normal $\mathbf n$ shown. Gray field arrows indicate direction only.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the supplied parameterization $x=\ln{\left(t \right)},\ y=2 t$, $1\le t\le e$. It runs from $(0,2)$ to $(1,2 e)$.

The tangent has direction $(\frac{1}{t},2)$. The pictured normal is its $90^\circ$ anticlockwise rotation, with direction $(-2,\frac{1}{t})$.

![Tangent and selected normal](flux-8afbb475ba53c9f4202d-orientation.png)

Substitute the curve into the field and differentiate its coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x(t),y(t))&=- 3 e^{- \left(\ln{\left(t \right)}\right)}=- \frac{3}{t} \\
Q(x(t),y(t))&=2 \\
x'&=\frac{1}{t} \\
y'&=2\end{aligned}
$$

The clockwise formula has the opposite normal, so negate it for the selected normal.

At positive endpoints use $\ln(1/u)=-\ln u$, $\ln u-\ln v=\ln(u/v)$, and $\ln e=1$ as needed; retain the logarithm terms in the final value.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds&=-\int_{1}^{e}(Py\prime-Qx\prime)\,\mathrm dt \\
&=-\int_{1}^{e}\left[\left(- \frac{3}{t}\right)(2)-(2)\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)\right]\,\mathrm dt \\
&=\int_{1}^{e}\left(\frac{8}{t}\right)\,\mathrm dt \\
&=\left[8 \ln{\left(t \right)}\right]_{1}^{e} \\
&=(8)-(0) \\
&=8\end{aligned}
$$

Use the supplied parameterization $x=\frac{1}{t},\ y=t$, $\frac{1}{2}\le t\le 2$. It runs from $(2,\frac{1}{2})$ to $(\frac{1}{2},2)$.

The tangent has direction $(- \frac{1}{t^{2}},1)$. The pictured normal is its $90^\circ$ anticlockwise rotation, with direction $(-1,- \frac{1}{t^{2}})$.

![Tangent and selected normal](flux-2f539ba3d37fb5f7f3d4-orientation.png)

Substitute the curve into the field and differentiate its coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x(t),y(t))&=2 \left(\frac{1}{t}\right)=\frac{2}{t} \\
Q(x(t),y(t))&=2 \left(t\right)^{2}=2 t^{2} \\
x'&=- \frac{1}{t^{2}} \\
y'&=1\end{aligned}
$$

The clockwise formula has the opposite normal, so negate it for the selected normal.

At positive endpoints use $\ln(1/u)=-\ln u$, $\ln u-\ln v=\ln(u/v)$, and $\ln e=1$ as needed; retain the logarithm terms in the final value.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds&=-\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{2}(Py\prime-Qx\prime)\,\mathrm dt \\
&=-\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{2}\left[\left(\frac{2}{t}\right)(1)-(2 t^{2})\left(- \frac{1}{t^{2}}\right)\right]\,\mathrm dt \\
&=\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{2}(-2 - \frac{2}{t})\,\mathrm dt \\
&=\left[- 2 t - 2 \ln{\left(t \right)}\right]_{\frac{1}{2}}^{2} \\
&=(-4 - 2 \ln{\left(2 \right)})-(-1 + 2 \ln{\left(2 \right)}) \\
&=-3 - 4 \ln{\left(2 \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Expressing Flux Over a Surface as a Repeated Integral

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨- x,\,- y + z,\,- x - y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=2 x - 2 y$ for $1\le x\le 4$ and $-1\le y\le 3.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{-1}^{3}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,2 u - 2 v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 4,\,-1\le v\le 3\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2 u - 2 v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,2⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2 u - 2 v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,\,2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨- x,\,- y + z,\,- x - y⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=2 u - 2 v} \\  & =⟨- u,\,- v + (2 u - 2 v),\,- u - v⟩ \\  & =⟨- u,\,2 u - 3 v,\,- u - v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨- u,\,2 u - 3 v,\,- u - v⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,2,\,1⟩ \\  & =(- u)\cdot (-2)+(2 u - 3 v)\cdot (2)+(- u - v)\cdot (1) \\  & =2 u+4 u - 6 v- u - v \\  & =5 u - 7 v.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨- x,\,- y + z,\,- x - y⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A. \\  & ={∬}_{D}(5 u - 7 v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{-1}^{3}(5 u - 7 v)\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Expressing Flux Over a Surface as a Repeated Integral

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨- 2 x - 2 z,\,- 2 y - 4 z,\,- 2 x + 8 y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=2 x + 4 y$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $-2\le y\le 5.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{5}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,2 u + 4 v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 3,\,-2\le v\le 5\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,\,-4,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}

$$

{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,uv + u - v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 3,\,-2\le v\le 5\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv + u - v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,v + 1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv + u - v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,u - 1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & v + 1 \\ 0 & 1 & u - 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & v + 1 \\ 1 & u - 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & v + 1 \\ 0 & u - 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨- v - 1,\,1 - u,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨2 z,\,2 xy,\,x + y⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=uv + u - v} \\  & =⟨2 (uv + u - v),\,2 uv,\,u + v⟩ \\  & =⟨2 uv + 2 u - 2 v,\,2 uv,\,u + v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨2 uv + 2 u - 2 v,\,2 uv,\,u + v⟩\cdot ⟨- v - 1,\,1 - u,\,1⟩ \\  & =(2 uv + 2 u - 2 v)\cdot (- v - 1)+(2 uv)\cdot (1 - u)+(u + v)\cdot (1) \\  & =- 2 uv^{2} - 4 uv - 2 u + 2 v^{2} + 2 v- 2 u^{2} v + 2 uv+u + v \\  & =- 2 u^{2} v - 2 uv^{2} - 2 uv - u + 2 v^{2} + 3 v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨2 z,\,2 xy,\,x + y⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A. \\  & ={∬}_{D}(- 2 u^{2} v - 2 uv^{2} - 2 uv - u + 2 v^{2} + 3 v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{5}(- 2 u^{2} v - 2 uv^{2} - 2 uv - u + 2 v^{2} + 3 v)\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Expressing Flux Over a Surface as a Repeated Integral

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨2 z,\,xy,\,x + y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=2 xy + x - y$ for $-2\le x\le 5$ and $-1\le y\le 2.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{-2}^{5}{\int }_{-1}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,2 uv + u - v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-2\le u\le 5,\,-1\le v\le 2\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2 uv + u - v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,2 v + 1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2 uv + u - v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2 u - 1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 2 v + 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 u - 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 v + 1 \\ 1 & 2 u - 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 v + 1 \\ 0 & 2 u - 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨- 2 v - 1,\,1 - 2 u,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨2 z,\,xy,\,x + y⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=2 uv + u - v} \\  & =⟨2 (2 uv + u - v),\,uv,\,u + v⟩ \\  & =⟨4 uv + 2 u - 2 v,\,uv,\,u + v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨4 uv + 2 u - 2 v,\,uv,\,u + v⟩\cdot ⟨- 2 v - 1,\,1 - 2 u,\,1⟩ \\  & =(4 uv + 2 u - 2 v)\cdot (- 2 v - 1)+(uv)\cdot (1 - 2 u)+(u + v)\cdot (1) \\  & =- 8 uv^{2} - 8 uv - 2 u + 4 v^{2} + 2 v- 2 u^{2} v + uv+u + v \\  & =- 2 u^{2} v - 8 uv^{2} - 7 uv - u + 4 v^{2} + 3 v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨2 z,\,xy,\,x + y⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A. \\  & ={∬}_{D}(- 2 u^{2} v - 8 uv^{2} - 7 uv - u + 4 v^{2} + 3 v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{5}{\int }_{-1}^{2}(- 2 u^{2} v - 8 uv^{2} - 7 uv - u + 4 v^{2} + 3 v)\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$
